en: What “porto” means and how we plan a season anywhere in Portugal. {0}

Porto Season plans long stays in Portugal: one to twelve months of living, working and slowing down in the country’s best towns, cities, coastlines and islands. We handle the hard parts so you can stay long enough to have a favorite café, a local market, and neighbors who know your name.

Most travel companies are built for a week. We’re built for a season. That changes everything: the home has to work on a Tuesday in February, the desk has to survive a long call, and someone has to know which pharmacy is open on Sunday.
One specialist plans your season end to end, from the first call to the day you leave, with partner lawyers for visas, vetted homes, workspaces, and a community waiting when you land.
We work across all of Portugal: not only Porto, but Lisbon, the coast, the Alentejo, the Douro, Madeira and the Azores.
— the place you sail into, drop anchor, and stay a while.

The quickest way to feel at home is to know your streets. From Alfama’s lanes in Lisbon to Bonfim in Porto and the old town of Funchal, we walk you through the bakeries, markets and corners that locals actually use.
Alfama at dawn: “Bread, fado and washing lines”

An early walk through Lisbon’s oldest quarter before the day-trippers arrive. We start with fresh bread and coffee, climb past the viewpoints and stop at a small fado house where the owner tells the neighborhood’s story. You finish knowing where to shop, eat and sit in the sun.
Porto beyond the river: “Bonfim and the quiet east”

A slow walk through Porto’s residential east, away from the Ribeira crowds. We visit a traditional grocer, a ceramics studio and a café where the same neighbors meet every morning. It is the best introduction to everyday Porto life.
Funchal market morning: “Fruit you have never tasted”

A morning in Funchal’s farmers’ market and the old town around it, tasting island fruit and learning what is in season. We finish on a street of painted doors with a cup of poncha or coffee. Practical tips on shopping and daily life are part of the walk.

Portugal has more than 800 kilometres of Atlantic coast. Learn to surf in Ericeira, swim in the warm lagoon waters off Tavira or watch whales from a small boat in the Azores, with people who know the sea well.
Ericeira surf month: “From foam to green waves”

Eight small-group lessons with a certified coach, matched to your level and the day’s conditions. Boards and wetsuits are included, and sessions move between beginner beaches and gentle reef breaks. By the end of the month most guests are catching unbroken waves on their own.
Ria Formosa by boat: “Islands, oysters and flamingos”

A small boat trip through the lagoon’s channels and salt marshes, with a local skipper who has fished here all his life. We stop on a barrier island to swim, visit an oyster farm and watch the birdlife. Bring a hat and a swimsuit.
Whales and dolphins: “Out into the open Atlantic”

A trip with a marine biologist on a small, responsibly run boat, guided by lookouts on the cliffs who spot the whales. Common dolphins are seen on most trips, and sperm whales are often present. Spring and summer bring the best chances of seeing migrating species.

Portuguese food is generous, seasonal and built on good markets. Cook with a home cook in Porto, learn the Alentejo’s slow-cooked dishes in Évora or simply learn to shop well at your local market in Lisbon.

Meet a home cook at the market hall, choose fish and vegetables together and learn how to tell what is fresh. Back in her kitchen you cook three classic dishes and sit down to eat them with a glass of wine. You go home with recipes and the confidence to shop like a local.

An evening of small plates at four family-run tascas, from bolinhos de bacalhau to slow-cooked tripe for the brave. Your guide explains the history of each dish and how to order without a menu. Drinks are included, and so is a final glass of tawny port.

A day in a farmhouse kitchen learning the Alentejo’s simple, herb-rich cooking: açorda, migas and slow-roasted pork. We bake bread in a wood oven and finish with a long lunch outdoors. A good way to understand why people here never rush a meal.

A little Portuguese changes everything, from the market to the neighbors. We arrange friendly group and private classes in Lisbon, Porto and Coimbra, plus language exchanges where you practise over coffee.
Portuguese for daily life: “Café, market, pharmacy”

A small group course focused on European Portuguese for real situations: ordering, shopping, small talk and appointments. Classes are two hours a week with a native teacher, plus short homework you can do on your commute. Most guests can manage everyday conversations by the end.

A relaxed weekly evening where Portuguese speakers who want to practise English meet guests who want to practise Portuguese. Tables switch language every half hour. It is the easiest way to make local friends.

Four hours of class each morning in a historic university town, with afternoon activities in Portuguese. You stay in a home in the old town and practise everywhere you go. Ideal for guests on a longer stay who want to make real progress quickly.
Portugal makes extraordinary wine at very fair prices. Spend a weekend in the Douro’s terraced vineyards, taste the bold reds of the Alentejo or join a harvest, guided by the families who make it.

Two days on a family quinta during the September harvest. You pick grapes in the morning, help with treading in the old stone lagares in the evening and share the workers’ lunch in between. Accommodation, meals and train tickets from Porto are included.
Alentejo wine and cork: “From oak to glass”

A day visiting a small winery that ages wine in clay amphorae, followed by a walk through a cork oak forest with a cork harvester. Lunch is at a country restaurant. You learn why the Alentejo landscape looks the way it does.
A private tasting in a family-owned port lodge, guided by the cellar master. You compare styles and ages and learn how port is made and blended. A good evening to bring visiting friends.
Some of Europe’s best walking is in Portugal. Follow Madeira’s levadas through laurel forest, walk the Rota Vicentina cliffs in the Algarve or hike between crater lakes in the Azores.
Levada walks: “Along the water, through the clouds”

A guided walk along one of Madeira’s historic irrigation channels, through laurel forest that has grown here for millions of years. Routes are chosen for your fitness and the day’s weather. Transport, snacks and a local guide are included.
Rota Vicentina weekend: “Cliffs and fishermen’s trails”

Two days walking the Fishermen’s Trail along the wild southwest coast, with luggage moved for you between guesthouses. Expect sandy paths, high cliffs and empty beaches. Dinner is fresh fish in a village restaurant.
Sete Cidades: “The rim of the crater”

A ridge walk around the huge Sete Cidades crater, looking down on its twin lakes, one blue and one green. The path is mostly gentle, and the views change with every cloud. We finish with a soak in a thermal pool.

Portugal’s hand-painted tiles cover churches, stations and ordinary houses. Learn to paint your own in Lisbon, throw pots with a ceramicist in Porto or meet the people who weave, carve and cork-craft across the country.
Paint your own azulejo: “Cobalt on white”

A small workshop with a tile painter, learning the traditional technique of painting cobalt blue onto glazed tiles. You design and paint your own tile, which is fired and ready to collect a week later. No drawing skills needed.

A six-week course in a small studio, learning to throw, trim and glaze your own cups and bowls. Classes are small and relaxed, and there is open studio time between sessions. You keep everything you make.
Cork craft day: “Bark that grows back”

Meet a craftsman who works with cork, learn how it is harvested every nine years without harming the tree, and make a small object of your own. The visit includes a walk among cork oaks. A good family activity.
A season is only as good as the people you share it with. In every destination, from Lisbon to Ericeira and Ponta do Sol, we host dinners, walks and coworking days that turn neighbors into friends.

A monthly dinner for guests, our local people and a few friends, around one long table in a family restaurant. It is simple, generous and the place where most friendships start. Partners and children are always welcome.

A weekly shared workday at a coworking space, with a group lunch in the middle. Bring your laptop and your questions about life in Portugal. It is an easy way to meet other remote workers without forcing it.
A weekly walk along the coast timed to the sunset, ending at a café or beach bar. Pace is gentle and everyone is welcome. Locals often join, especially in summer.

Madeira and the Azores are Portugal at its most dramatic: volcanic, green and surrounded by deep ocean. Swim in natural lava pools, soak in hot springs in Furnas or settle into Ponta do Sol’s remote-work community.
Furnas hot springs: “Stew from the ground”

A day in the volcanic valley of Furnas, watching cozido stew being lifted out of the hot earth where it has cooked for hours. After lunch, soak in warm, iron-rich thermal pools in a botanical garden. Bring a dark swimsuit, because the water stains.

A drive along Madeira’s north coast to the natural lava pools of Porto Moniz, with stops at waterfalls and viewpoints on the way. Swim in calm, sea-filled pools sheltered from the waves. Lunch is grilled fish in a fishing village.
Ponta do Sol: “A week to settle in”

A first week designed for island life: an introduction to the remote-work community, a bus and car-hire briefing, a market morning and a first levada walk. You end the week with friends and a routine. Included in every Madeira stay.
Seven hills, river light and a café on every corner.

Lisbon is a capital that still feels walkable, with trams climbing past tiled façades and viewpoints at the top of almost every street. You can work from a sunny apartment in the morning, eat grilled sardines at lunch and be on a beach by the Tagus estuary within half an hour. It is the easiest place in Portugal to arrive, settle and meet people quickly.
People who want a real city rhythm, good food and an easy social life, with the sea never far away.
Leafy squares, independent shops and quiet streets a short walk from Bairro Alto’s evenings.
A flat, residential grid with a great market hall, bakeries and an easy family feel.
The oldest quarter: steep lanes, washing lines, fado on warm nights and river views.
Fibre is standard in most central buildings, with 500 Mbps to 1 Gbps common. Mobile 5G coverage is strong.
The largest remote-work and expat community in Portugal, with meetups, language exchanges and coworking events most nights of the week.
Granite, river mist and port lodges glowing at dusk.

Porto is compact, hilly and full of character, built in granite and azulejo along the Douro river. Life here is a little calmer and a little cheaper than in Lisbon, with a strong local identity and a serious food scene. The Atlantic beaches of Foz and Matosinhos are a short bus ride from the centre.
People who like a city with texture and a slightly slower pace, and who don’t mind a rainier winter in exchange for it.
A residential, creative neighborhood with new cafés, galleries and calm streets east of the centre.
Design shops, small restaurants and easy access to everything, ten minutes’ walk from the river.
Where the river meets the ocean: seafront walks, sunsets and a quieter, village feel.
Fibre is widely available across the city. Older granite buildings can have thick walls, so we check Wi-Fi in every room.
A growing, friendly remote-work scene, plus a strong arts and university crowd. Easier to get to know locals than in Lisbon.
Seaside promenades, forested hills and Lisbon 40 minutes away.

Cascais is a polished seaside town with a long coastal promenade, sheltered beaches and a direct train to Lisbon. Inland, the hills of Sintra are cooler and greener, full of palaces, misty forest trails and old quintas. Together they offer a calmer, outdoor life with the capital close enough for a day.
Families and couples who want safe streets, beaches and good schools nearby, without giving up city access.
Walk to the beach, the market and the train, with cafés and restaurants on every street.
Residential and green, with a long seafront path linking small beaches all the way to Cascais.
Cooler, wooded and romantic, with palaces above and hiking trails from the doorstep.
Fibre is standard in Cascais and Estoril. A few rural Sintra properties rely on 4G or 5G routers, which we test before you arrive.
A settled international community, many of them families, with clubs, sailing, surf schools and weekend markets.
A whitewashed fishing town on a world-class surf coast.

Ericeira is a small fishing town of white and blue houses above the Atlantic, at the heart of a protected surf reserve. Mornings start with checking the waves, days are for work or long cliff walks, and evenings end with fresh fish by the harbour. Lisbon is about 50 minutes away by car or bus.
Anyone who wants the ocean to set the rhythm of their days, from first-time surfers to people taking a proper break.
Cobbled lanes, small squares and sea views, with everything within a few minutes’ walk.
A quiet village just north of town, close to the main reef breaks.
A wide river-mouth beach to the south, good for beginners and long evening walks.
Fibre covers the town itself. Outlying villas can be slower, so we list a tested speed for every home.
A tight, outdoorsy community of surfers, remote workers and young families. Easy to meet people in the water or at the weekly dinners.
Rice fields, pine forest and empty white beaches.

Comporta is a string of low-key villages between rice paddies, cork and pine forest and a long Atlantic beach. Life is barefoot and unhurried, with storks on the chimneys and sandy roads to the sea. It is quiet outside summer, which is exactly why people come.
People who want nature and space more than nightlife, and who are happy to drive for supplies and company.
The small centre, with a few restaurants, a grocery and the rice museum.
A quieter village to the south with access to wide, empty beaches.
Rolling hills, a lagoon by the sea and a growing creative community.
Fibre is reaching more homes, but many rural houses use 4G or 5G routers. We test every home and add a backup router where needed.
Small and seasonal. Off-season it is a handful of creatives, families and long-stayers, and we organise regular dinners to bring them together.
Golden cliffs, sea caves and a lively harbour town.

Lagos is a historic walled town with a busy marina and some of the most dramatic coastline in Europe: ochre cliffs, grottoes and sheltered coves. West of town the coast turns wild towards Sagres and the Costa Vicentina, with surf, hiking and very few buildings. Winters are mild and sunny, which makes it a favourite for long stays.
People who want sunshine most of the year, an active outdoor life and an easy, sociable town.
Inside and around the old walls: markets, cafés and the beach a few minutes away.
A relaxed village with a long beach and a strong family and international community.
The southwestern tip of Europe, wind-swept and surf-focused, with huge skies.
Fibre is widely available in Lagos and Luz. Some rural homes towards Sagres rely on 5G routers.
A big, friendly international community of surfers, sailors, families and remote workers, with plenty of meetups year-round.
A quiet river town, salt pans and warm island beaches.

Tavira is one of the prettiest towns in the Algarve: a Roman bridge, church towers, hipped roofs and a river running into the Ria Formosa lagoon. The beaches are on barrier islands reached by small ferries, and the sea is the warmest in mainland Portugal. It is calm, traditional and very easy to live in.
People who want warm weather, a gentle pace and a real Portuguese town rather than a resort.
Both banks of the river, with the market, cafés and ferries to the island beaches.
A small fishing village known for octopus, with a waterfront promenade.
A relaxed lagoon village facing a long island beach, popular with families.
Fibre in town and most surrounding villages. Expect reliable speeds for video calls.
A settled community of long-stayers and retirees, plus local life that carries on all year. Smaller and quieter than the western Algarve.
A walled Roman town in a sea of cork oaks and vines.

Évora is a UNESCO-listed university town with a Roman temple, whitewashed lanes and a lively main square, surrounded by the rolling plains of the Alentejo. Days are slow and generous, built around long lunches, local wine and country walks among cork oaks and olive groves. In 2027 the town is European Capital of Culture, with a year-long programme of events.
People who want space, quiet and culture at a gentle price, and who enjoy the countryside more than the beach.
The historic centre, with the Praça do Giraldo, the cathedral and everything on foot.
Quintas and farmhouses among cork oaks, ten to twenty minutes from town by car.
A tiny hilltop village above the Alqueva lake, famous for its dark, starry skies.
Fibre is good in town. Rural quintas often use 5G routers, which we test and back up before you arrive.
A university town with a young local crowd and a small but growing international community, set to be busier during the 2027 culture year.
Terraced vineyards falling steeply to a slow green river.

The Douro Valley is one of the oldest wine regions in the world, with hand-built terraces stepping down to the river for mile after mile. Small villages, family quintas and riverside railway stations set the scale of daily life. It is deeply peaceful, especially outside the harvest, and Porto is under two hours away by train.
People who want deep quiet and beautiful views to write, think or simply rest, with wine as a very pleasant side effect.
A small riverside village at the heart of the valley, with a tiled train station.
The largest town in the valley, with shops, a market and good rail links to Porto.
A handsome cathedral town on the south bank, with a famous baroque stairway.
Variable. Village homes often have fibre, while hillside quintas use 4G or 5G. We only offer homes that pass a video-call test.
Small and rural. Most of your community will be winemakers, neighbors and fellow guests, and we organise regular get-togethers.
A university hill town of libraries, river walks and student songs.

Coimbra is home to one of the oldest universities in Europe, set on a hill above the Mondego river. It is a real Portuguese city with a young population, affordable living and very little tourist gloss. The coast at Figueira da Foz is under an hour away, and both Lisbon and Porto are easy by fast train.
People who want to live like a local, learn Portuguese properly and keep costs down, in a city with real history.
The old upper town around the university, with steep lanes and wide views.
The lower town: shops, cafés and the riverside, flat and easy to get around.
Across the river, quieter and residential, with green parks and city views.
Fibre is standard across the city, with reliable speeds for calls and uploads.
Mostly local and academic. Language exchanges and university events make it easy to meet Portuguese people rather than only other visitors.
Spring all year, cliffside levadas and Atlantic sunsets.

Madeira is a volcanic island of steep green mountains, banana terraces and walking trails that follow old irrigation channels called levadas. Funchal is a proper small city with markets, gardens and a harbour, while Ponta do Sol on the sunny south coast has an established remote-work community. Temperatures barely change through the year, so winter here feels like late spring.
People who want mild weather all year, outdoor adventure on the doorstep and an easy community from the first week.
Painted doors, the farmers’ market and the seafront, with everything on foot.
A small, sunny village on the south coast, popular with remote workers.
Further west, with a sheltered sandy beach, a marina and quiet hillside homes.
Fibre in Funchal and most of the south coast. Mountain villages can be patchier, which we flag on each home.
One of the best-organised remote-work communities in Europe, especially around Ponta do Sol, plus a long-standing international crowd in Funchal.
Crater lakes, hot springs and whales in the open Atlantic.

São Miguel is the largest island of the Azores, halfway between Europe and North America. It is intensely green, with volcanic crater lakes, tea plantations, thermal pools and dairy pastures running down to the sea. Ponta Delgada is a small, friendly city, and the rest of the island is a short drive away.
People who love nature and changeable weather, and want somewhere truly different without leaving Portugal or the EU.

What is included in a plan?

Every plan includes a vetted home, a proper place to work, airport pickup, a local SIM, a welcome week and our community events. Longer plans add help with your NIF and local admin, planned weekend escapes and, for Full year and Family season, visa guidance with our partner immigration lawyers. Family season also includes school guidance. Flights, food, everyday spending and optional experiences are not included unless we say so.
How does my specialist work with me?

You have one dedicated specialist from your first call to the day you leave. They help you choose a destination and home, coordinate visa guidance and school visits where relevant, and stay in touch by email or video call throughout your stay. Our local hosts take care of things on the ground, and your specialist makes sure nothing falls between the gaps.
Is the internet good enough for remote work?

Yes. We test the connection in every home before we offer it and list the measured speed on each listing. Most city homes have fibre at 500 Mbps or more. Rural and island homes can be slower, so where needed we add a backup 4G or 5G router. Every destination also has a coworking option nearby, and we can arrange a membership for you.
Should I rent monthly or sign a yearly lease?

For stays of up to three months, a furnished monthly rental is usually simplest and gives you flexibility. For six months or more, a longer lease almost always costs less per month and is often needed for residence applications. We negotiate either on your behalf, check the contract and explain the terms in plain English before you sign.
When is the best time to go?

It depends on where. Lisbon and Porto are lovely from March to June and September to November. The Algarve has mild, sunny winters, which makes it a favorite from October to April. The Alentejo and the Douro are best in spring and autumn, as July and August can pass 35°C. Madeira is pleasant all year, and the Azores are greenest and calmest from May to October. Each destination page shows typical temperatures and rainfall by month.

Not in Lisbon, Porto or Coimbra, which have good public transport and fast trains between them. On the coast, in the countryside and on the islands a car makes life much easier, and in Comporta, the Douro and the Azores it is close to essential. We can arrange a long-term rental. Licences from many countries can be used for a limited period, and residents may need to exchange theirs, so check the rules for your licence with us before you travel.

Portugal has good public and private healthcare. For short stays you need comprehensive travel or international health insurance, and visa applications normally require proof of health cover. EU travelers can use their European Health Insurance Card for necessary care. Residents can register with the local health centre once their residence is in place. We can point you to clinics, pharmacies and English-speaking doctors in every destination.
What happens if something goes wrong during my stay?

Contact your specialist or local host at any time. If the boiler breaks, we arrange a repair. If a home falls short of what we promised, we fix it or move you. For anything urgent at night or at weekends, there is an emergency line for guests in season. In a medical emergency, call 112 first, then let us know so we can help.

Start with the season planner or a call with a specialist. We send you a written proposal with homes, dates and a full price. When you are happy, you confirm with a deposit and we reserve your home. Visa guidance, school visits and admin are then scheduled in the months before you arrive.
How do payments and deposits work?

We ask for a [30]% deposit to confirm your plan and reserve your home. The balance for your first month is due [60] days before arrival, and for longer stays each following month is paid [30] days in advance. A refundable damage deposit of [one month’s rent] is held for the home and returned within [30] days of departure. Exact terms are set out in your proposal.
Which currencies can I pay in?

All prices are set in euros. You can view approximate prices in other currencies on the site, but invoices are issued in euros and payable by bank transfer or card. Card payments may carry a [X]% fee.
What is not included in the price?

Flights, food, local transport, optional experiences with a listed price, visa application fees, lawyers’ fees for the application itself and school fees are not included. Utilities are included for stays up to three months and, for longer leases, are usually paid directly. Your proposal lists exactly what is and is not covered.
Can the price change after I book?

No. Once your deposit is paid, the price for the confirmed dates and home is fixed. The only exceptions are changes you ask for, such as extra months or a different home, and government fees outside our control.

If you cancel more than [90] days before arrival, we refund everything except a [€500] planning fee. Between [90] and [30] days, we keep the [30]% deposit. Within [30] days, the first month is non-refundable. If your visa is refused despite a complete application, we refund [all payments except the planning fee]. These terms are placeholders and will be confirmed in your proposal.
Can I change destination halfway through my season?

Yes, and many guests do: a few months in Lisbon followed by a few on the coast or in Madeira is a lovely way to see more of Portugal. Tell us as early as you can, ideally [30] days ahead. We find the new home, move you and adjust the price to match.

Usually, yes, subject to the home’s availability and your immigration status. If you are visiting under short-stay rules, remember the {schengenDays}-day limit in any {schengenWindow}-day period. Staying longer than that needs a national visa, which must be applied for in advance. Your specialist will tell you what is possible before you commit.
What if I need to leave early?

Life happens. If you need to leave early, let your specialist know. Months already paid are non-refundable, but we will try to re-let the home and refund [50]% of any recovered rent. We strongly recommend travel insurance that covers curtailment.

Yes. We ask every guest to have travel insurance that covers cancellation, curtailment and medical care from the day they book. For residence visas, specific health cover is usually required as well, and our partner lawyers will tell you what is accepted.
How long can I stay without a visa?

If you hold a passport that is visa-exempt for the Schengen area, such as a US, UK, Canadian or Australian passport, you can stay up to {schengenDays} days in any {schengenWindow}-day period. That limit covers the whole Schengen area, not just Portugal, and it is a rolling window, so recent trips count. Our Taster and Season plans are designed to fit within it. To stay longer you need a national visa, applied for before you travel. This is guidance only, not legal advice.
What is the difference between the D8 and the D7 visa?

The D8, often called the digital nomad visa, is for people working remotely for employers or clients outside Portugal. The D7 is for people with regular passive income, such as pensions, rental income, dividends or royalties. Both can lead to residence. Which one fits depends on your income, work and plans, and our partner immigration lawyers, {visaPartner}, will confirm the right route for you. This is guidance only, not legal advice.
How much income do I need for a D8 or D7 visa?

The D8 currently requires remote-work income of at least {d8Income} a month for a single applicant, which is four times the Portuguese minimum wage. The D7 threshold is linked to the minimum wage, currently around {d7Income} a month for a single applicant. Both rise when the minimum wage rises, and extra amounts apply for a partner and children. Savings and other evidence may also be considered. Your figures will be confirmed by our partner lawyers, {visaPartner}. This is guidance only, not legal advice.
Do you handle my visa application?

We guide you, but we do not submit visa applications ourselves. Applications are prepared and handled by our partner immigration lawyers, {visaPartner}, who are qualified to advise on your case. We help you understand the options, gather documents, and coordinate timings with your home and plan. Final requirements always come from the Portuguese consulate and AIMA. This is guidance only, not legal advice.
Do I need a NIF and a Portuguese bank account?

A NIF is your Portuguese tax number, and you need one for almost everything: a lease, utilities, a phone contract and opening a bank account. Non-residents can get one through a fiscal representative, which we help arrange. A Portuguese bank account is usually required for visa applications and makes paying rent and bills much easier. We help with both as part of the Season, Full year and Family season plans.

EES, the EU Entry/Exit System, is now in operation. Non-EU travelers register fingerprints and a facial image at the border on their first entry, replacing passport stamps. ETIAS is a separate online travel authorization for visa-exempt travelers, with a fee of {etiasFee}. It is currently {etiasStatus}. Only ever apply through the official EU travel portal. This is guidance only, not legal advice.
Will I have to pay tax in Portugal?

It depends on how long you stay, where you are tax resident and your home country’s rules. Spending more than 183 days in Portugal in a year, or having a habitual residence here, can make you tax resident. We do not give tax advice. Please speak to a qualified tax adviser in Portugal and in your home country before you commit to a long stay, and we are happy to introduce you to one.
What are the options for schools?

Lisbon, Cascais, Porto, the Algarve and Madeira have international schools with British, American and IB curricula, and many children also thrive in Portuguese state or private schools. Places at popular international schools can be limited, so start early, ideally six to nine months ahead. On the Family season plan we help you shortlist schools, arrange visits and manage applications. Fees are paid directly to the school.
Can we come for just one school term?

Yes. Many international schools accept students for a single term, and a term of three to four months is our most popular family season. Note that a stay longer than {schengenDays} days in any {schengenWindow}-day period needs a national visa for visa-exempt travelers, so a full term may require one. We will help you plan dates and visas together.
Can you plan a season for someone with access needs?

Yes. Tell us what you need and we will only suggest homes that meet it, with step-free access, lifts, walk-in showers or ground-floor bedrooms where required. Some towns, such as Lisbon and Porto, are very hilly and have uneven cobbled streets, while others, like Tavira and Campo de Ourique in Lisbon, are flatter. We will be honest about what each place is like.
Can I bring my dog or cat?

Often, yes. Some of our homes accept pets, and Portugal is generally dog-friendly. Pets travelling from outside the EU need a microchip, a rabies vaccination and an animal health certificate, and some countries require a blood test months in advance. We will match you with pet-friendly homes and point you to vets in your destination.
Can you arrange childcare and activities?

Yes. We can introduce you to vetted babysitters and nannies, holiday camps and after-school clubs, from surf and football to music and art. Portuguese family life is very child-friendly, and children are welcome in almost every restaurant.
How do you handle my documents and personal data?

Passport scans, income documents and visa paperwork are stored encrypted and shared only with our partner immigration lawyers, {visaPartner}, when you ask us to. Access is logged, and we never sell or share your data for marketing. You can ask us to delete your documents at any time, and we will do so within {deletionDays} days, unless the law requires us to keep something.
Do I need to speak Portuguese?

No, especially in Lisbon, Porto and the Algarve, where English is widely spoken. But a little Portuguese goes a long way, particularly in smaller towns and with older neighbors. We offer classes and language exchanges in every plan, and locals really appreciate the effort.
I am an EU citizen. Is anything different?

Yes, it is much simpler. EU, EEA and Swiss citizens can live in Portugal without a visa. For stays over three months you register your residence with the local council. Everything else in our plans, from the home to the community, works in the same way.
What time zone is Portugal in?

Mainland Portugal and Madeira are on Western European Time, the same as the UK, with summer time from late March to late October. The Azores are one hour behind. That makes Portugal convenient for working with Europe, and overlaps with the US East Coast in the afternoon.

The terms on which {0} plans and arranges tailor-made journeys. Please read them before you confirm a booking.

These terms apply to every journey arranged by {0} (“we”, “us”), contact {1}, {2}. “You” means the person making the booking and everyone travelling on it. The person who makes the booking confirms that they are authorised to accept these terms on behalf of everyone named on it.

Every journey starts with an enquiry and a conversation. We then send a written proposal with an itinerary and a quote. Proposals and quotes are free and are not a booking: places are not held until a booking is confirmed, and availability and prices can change until then.

Our quotes are tailor-made and state what is and is not included. Unless the quote says otherwise, international flights, travel insurance, visas, tips, and personal expenses are not included. Once a booking is confirmed we will not change its price except where permitted by law, for example because of changes in transport costs, taxes or fees imposed by third parties or exchange rates, and we will tell you as early as possible and explain how the change was calculated.
A booking is confirmed when you accept the proposal, pay the deposit stated in it and we send you a written confirmation. The deposit secures the arrangements and is used to pay suppliers.

The balance is due by the date stated in your confirmation, usually some weeks before you travel. If the balance is not received on time we may treat the booking as cancelled by you and apply the cancellation charges below. Bookings made close to departure may require full payment at the time of booking.

If you want to change your booking after it is confirmed, tell us in writing as soon as possible. We will do our best to help, but changes depend on availability and suppliers’ own conditions. We will pass on any extra cost and may charge a reasonable fee for the work involved; both will be agreed with you before we make the change.

You may transfer your booking to another person who meets any conditions of the journey, provided you give us reasonable notice before departure. You and the new traveller are jointly responsible for any balance and for any extra costs arising from the transfer.

You may cancel at any time by writing to us. Because we pay suppliers in advance, cancellation charges apply; they increase as departure gets closer and are set out in your proposal and confirmation before you book. Where suppliers refund us, we will pass the refund on to you less the cancellation charge. Your travel insurance may cover cancellation charges in some circumstances.

You may cancel without a charge if unavoidable and extraordinary circumstances at your destination significantly affect the journey, such as war, natural disaster or a serious outbreak of disease, as recognised by the relevant government travel advice.

We plan carefully, but occasionally we have to make changes. If a change is minor we will tell you as soon as we can. If we have to make a significant change, or cancel your journey, we will tell you as soon as possible and offer you the choice of the changed arrangements, an alternative journey of equivalent or higher standard if available, or a full refund of the money you have paid us.
We will not cancel your journey after the balance is due unless we are forced to by unavoidable and extraordinary circumstances, or because you have not paid.

Comprehensive travel insurance is a condition of booking. It must cover cancellation and curtailment, medical treatment, repatriation and any activities included in your journey. Please arrange it when you book and send us the policy details before you travel.

Each traveller is responsible for holding a valid passport, any visas and entry permits, and meeting the health and vaccination requirements for every country on the itinerary, including any rules on passport validity and blank pages. We will share general guidance, but requirements change: please check the official government advice for your nationality before you book and again before you travel. We are not responsible for costs arising from missing or incorrect documents.
Please tell us before you book about any medical condition, disability or reduced mobility that may affect your journey, so that we can advise whether the arrangements are suitable.

We are responsible for making sure that the arrangements we book are provided as described, by suppliers we have selected with reasonable care. If something goes wrong, tell us or the supplier straight away so that it can be put right.

We are not responsible where a failure is caused by you, by a third party not connected with providing your journey, or by unavoidable and extraordinary circumstances beyond our control. Where we are liable, our liability is limited as permitted by law and by the international conventions that apply to air, sea and rail travel and to hotels. Nothing in these terms limits liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence, or any other liability that cannot be limited by law.
Excursions or services that you book directly with a local supplier during your journey are not part of our arrangements, and we are not responsible for them.

We ask you to follow the reasonable instructions of our suppliers, respect local laws and customs, and not behave in a way that puts others at risk or causes damage. We may end the journey of anyone who does, without refund.

If you have a problem during your journey, tell the supplier and us at once so that we can try to resolve it on the spot. If it is not resolved, write to us at {0} within 28 days of your return and we will reply promptly. If we cannot agree, you may be able to use an alternative dispute resolution scheme.

These terms are governed by the law that applies where our business is established, and any dispute will be dealt with by the courts there. This does not take away any protection given to you by the mandatory consumer laws of the country where you live.
